title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+L)^c.\]
Here \(L\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
definitions:
Instance and encoding. There is one weight \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for each unordered pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), and no loops. Weights are exact integers of arbitrary finite bit length. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\). Define the self-delimiting code
\[U(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t).\]
The input is \(U(n)\) followed by \(U(a_{ij})\) in lexicographic order of \((i,j)\), for all \(1\le i<j\le n\). Its length in bits is \(L\). No matrix entry is supplied implicitly by an oracle or by a succinct circuit.

Objective and output. A tour is any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), interpreted cyclically. Set \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). Its cost and the optimum are
\[\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{\pi(i),\pi(i+1)},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(a)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi),\]
where \(S_n\) is the finite set of all such permutations. The graph is complete, so a tour always exists and the minimum is attained. The output is the explicit list of its \(n\) vertex labels, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Any minimum-cost tour is accepted, including any rotation or reversal of one; no uniqueness is required. An invalid list, an explicit failure output, or a suboptimal tour counts as failure. Returning only the optimum value, a bound or an approximate tour is not the required output.

Machine and charges. Use a word RAM whose word length on this input is
\[w=B\left\lceil n+\log_2(L+2)\right\rceil\text{ bits}.\]
The algorithm has one finite program independent of \(n,L\) and all weights. A word is an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); a memory address is one word. The input bits are packed in order into consecutive read-only words, padding the last word with zeros and exposing the true input length. Working memory is initially zero and contains no advice or precomputed tables. Reading or writing one addressed word, copying a word, comparing two words, branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and a left or right shift by a word-specified amount each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\) and cost one operation; integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one operation. Division by zero is not permitted. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one operation. Outputting a word, including the final partial word, costs one operation.

Integers longer than one word must be represented and processed using multiple charged operations; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers or exact real numbers. Reading and decoding the input, constructing tables, generating random bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing the entire tour are included in the clock. Addressing exponential-size subset tables is allowed by the linear-in-\(n\) word length. There is no separate polynomial-space restriction, and no quantum memory, quantum query, advice string or ideal oracle. The fixed polynomial overhead permitted in \(n+L\) accommodates the bit cost of operations on these finite-width words; this does not assert that sequential simulation of arbitrary random memory access has only polynomial overhead.

Probability and uniformity. For each fixed input the probability is over the machine’s independent fair coin stream. The same success guarantee holds on every input, not just on average over a distribution of weights. The running-time bound holds for every possible coin stream, including unsuccessful executions, so it is a worst-case clock rather than an expected-time bound. The constants \(\varepsilon,K,c,B\) cannot depend on the weights, their range or any property of the instance.

Scope. There is no triangle inequality, Euclidean geometry, bounded-weight, small-doubling or other structural promise. Polynomial dependence on \(L\) is allowed; polynomial dependence on the numerical maximum or sum of the weights is not automatically allowed. The fixed saving \(\varepsilon>0\) cannot tend to zero with \(n\).
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive proof must specify one uniform classical algorithm and fixed constants, prove the worst-case clock including input and output costs, and prove per-instance success probability at least \(2/3\) for an exactly optimal tour. A negative proof must exclude every such algorithm and every permitted choice of constants in the stated randomized word-RAM model. A conditional lower bound settles only that conditional assertion. A restriction on one dynamic-programming framework, a local-search rule or a polynomial-space algorithm does not exclude all allowed algorithms. Faster Hamiltonicity detection, pseudo-polynomial dependence on weight magnitudes, a restricted weight class, approximate optimization or a quantum algorithm does not meet the full positive target.
why: Exact weighted TSP is a basic test of whether optimization over all orders of a set fundamentally requires base-two exponential time. A fixed reduction of that base would save an exponential factor for every sufficiently large instance, even when costs have arbitrary binary representations. Understanding this boundary would distinguish the difficulty of selecting an optimal tour from the already faster task of merely detecting a tour.

importance.reason: A central exact-algorithm question with a sixty-year base-two barrier and a modern improvement that carefully distinguishes prefactor from exponent. It is separate from metric TSP approximation and from Hamiltonian-cycle detection.

progress.text: Bellman and Held–Karp establish the classical subset-based exact algorithm, recalled by the modern primary paper.
Undirected Hamiltonicity receives a sub-two-base Monte Carlo algorithm; the weighted extension retains pseudo-polynomial dependence on total weight.
Stoian’s revised paper reduces the prefactor of the historical exact TSP bound while retaining exponential base two.
SODA local-search lower bounds concern specified k-opt processes, not all exact algorithms.
The STACS small-doubling theorem extends the faster weighted regime under a fixed structural promise on the weight set.
New classical time-space tradeoffs improve interior points above time base two.
A further improvement nearly determines the best time-space product within the chain-based framework.
A quantum extension uses quantum search and QRAM.
The ESA quantum tradeoff paper is published with an explicit QRAM requirement.

context_blocks.text: In a complete graph the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle is automatic. The difficulty is selecting the cheapest one among the possible orders. Two tours with almost identical edges can have very different costs, and there is no restriction tying those costs to a geometric distance. The card therefore concerns exact optimization rather than finding any spanning cycle.

The Bellman and Held–Karp algorithms from 1962 give the familiar \(O(2^n n^2)\) arithmetic-operation bound. Stoian’s 2024 result improves this to deterministic time \(2^n n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in its stated model. This is a real improvement to the long-standing bound, but its exponent is still \(n-o(n)\). It does not give a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\) in \((2-\varepsilon)^n\). Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.

source_formulation.text: Preserves importance 96 and the existing editorial choice of complete symmetric TSP with arbitrary nonnegative binary integer weights, bounded-error classical randomization, a worst-case clock and polynomial bit-length overhead. Retains the random-access model with word length proportional to n+log(L), so the statement does not silently replace exponential-space random access by a slower sequential machine. Stoian’s 2024 question concerns the prefactor of the historical bound; the broader fixed-base question is explicitly discussed as open in Dallant–Kozma and the July 2026 follow-up.

sentences: Exact weighted TSP asks for a cheapest tour through every vertex of a complete undirected graph.
This question seeks a uniform classical algorithm with a fixed exponential time base below two.
Weights are arbitrary nonnegative integers written in binary, and only polynomial dependence on their total encoding length is allowed.
Bounded-error randomization and exponential memory are permitted, but every execution must satisfy the stated worst-case clock.
Recent prefactor, structured-weight, time-space and quantum improvements do not establish the full classical guarantee.
